config.title: Cookie-Based Auth Flow

intro.title: Cookie-Based Auth Flow
intro.body: In this lesson, you will build a simple React application that simulates a cookie-based authentication flow. You will learn how to manage user login and logout states, and conditionally render content based on whether a user is authenticated. The core programming concepts used are React state management with the useState hook and conditional rendering. You will work with JSX for the user interface and handle basic click events to update the application's state. This hands-on project will help you understand how authentication status can control what users see in a web application.
intro.usecase: Cookie-based authentication is the foundation of session management in countless web applications. When you log into platforms like GitHub, Notion, or banking dashboards, your browser stores an authentication cookie that keeps you logged in across page refreshes and navigation. As a developer, implementing this flow means creating login forms that securely exchange credentials for cookies, protecting user dashboards and admin panels from unauthorized access. This pattern is essential for any application requiring persistent user sessions without exposing tokens in client-side JavaScript.

objectives: Construct a React component to render a login form with controlled inputs.
Initialize and manage authentication state using the useState hook.
Implement a form submission handler to send user credentials to a mock API endpoint.
Configure an HTTP request to set authentication cookies in the browser.
Apply conditional rendering to display user-specific content based on authentication state.
Integrate a logout handler to clear authentication cookies and reset state.
Manipulate the DOM to conditionally show login or logout UI elements.

steps.title: Import React and useState
steps.instruction: Import React and the useState hook from the 'react' package.
steps.hint: Use the import statement to bring in React and useState from 'react'.
steps.analogousExample:
// Example: importing React and a hook
import React, { useState } from 'react';
steps.expectedOutcome: The React library and useState hook are available for use in your component.
successCriteria: React and useState are imported from 'react'.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully imported React and useState.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close. Make sure you're importing both React and useState from 'react'.
steps.feedbackWrong: That's not quite right. You need to import React and useState from the 'react' package.

steps.title: Create the main Auth component
steps.instruction: Create a functional component named Auth that returns an empty div element.
steps.hint: Define a function called Auth that returns a JSX div element.
steps.seedCode:
import React, { useState } from 'react';
// Create the Auth component here
steps.expectedOutcome: The Auth component is defined and returns an empty div.
successCriteria: A functional component named Auth is created and returns a div element.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close. Make sure you've defined a function named Auth that returns a div element.
steps.feedbackWrong: The Auth component isn't defined correctly. Create a function named Auth that returns a div element.

steps.title: Initialize authentication state
steps.instruction: Inside your Auth component, use useState to create an isLoggedIn state variable initialized to false.
steps.hint: Call useState with false as the initial value and destructure the returned array into isLoggedIn and setIsLoggedIn.
steps.expectedOutcome: The Auth component will have an isLoggedIn state variable initialized to false, ready to track authentication status.
successCriteria: The Auth component contains a useState call that initializes isLoggedIn to false.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure you're using useState with false as the initial value and destructuring the array into isLoggedIn and setIsLoggedIn.
steps.feedbackWrong: Inside the Auth component, use useState(false) to create an isLoggedIn state variable.

steps.title: Create login handler function
steps.instruction: Inside your Auth component, define a function named handleLogin that sets isLoggedIn to true, sets username to 'JohnDoe', and simulates setting a cookie by logging 'Cookie set' to the console.
steps.hint: Create a function that updates both state variables and logs a message. Place it before the return statement.
steps.expectedOutcome: You will have a handleLogin function that updates authentication state and logs a cookie simulation.
successCriteria: The handleLogin function is defined, sets isLoggedIn to true, sets username to 'JohnDoe', and logs 'Cookie set' to the console.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You've defined the function, but it's missing one or more required actions: setting isLoggedIn to true, setting username to 'JohnDoe', or logging 'Cookie set'.
steps.feedbackWrong: The handleLogin function is not defined or doesn't perform the required actions. Make sure it sets both state variables and logs the cookie simulation.

steps.title: Create logout handler function
steps.instruction: Define a handleLogout function inside your Auth component that sets isLoggedIn to false, sets username to an empty string, and logs a message about removing a cookie.
steps.hint: Add a new function after your handleLogin function. Use setIsLoggedIn(false) and setUsername(''). Include a console.log to simulate cookie removal.
steps.expectedOutcome: Your component will have a handleLogout function that updates both state variables and logs a message.
successCriteria: A handleLogout function is defined that sets isLoggedIn to false, sets username to '', and logs a message about cookie removal.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You've created a logout handler, but make sure it sets both isLoggedIn to false and username to an empty string, and includes a console.log message.
steps.feedbackWrong: The logout handler is missing or incomplete. Create a function named handleLogout that updates both state variables and logs a message.

steps.title: Add conditional rendering structure
steps.instruction: Inside your Auth component's return statement, replace the current null with a div containing a ternary operator that checks the isLoggedIn state. When true, render a paragraph saying 'Welcome back, [username]!', and when false, render a paragraph saying 'Please log in.'
steps.hint: Use the ternary operator syntax: condition ? expressionIfTrue : expressionIfFalse. Wrap the entire ternary in a div element.
steps.expectedOutcome: The component now returns a div with a ternary operator that conditionally displays a welcome message or a login prompt based on the isLoggedIn state.
successCriteria: The return statement contains a div wrapping a ternary operator that checks isLoggedIn and renders appropriate paragraph elements for both true and false cases.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but check that you have both true and false branches in your ternary operator, and that they're wrapped in a div element.
steps.feedbackWrong: The conditional rendering structure isn't quite right. Make sure you're using a ternary operator to check isLoggedIn and returning paragraph elements inside a div.

steps.title: Create login form markup
steps.instruction: In the false branch of your existing ternary (where isLoggedIn is false), add a login form with a heading, an input field, and a login button.
steps.hint: The false branch currently returns null. Replace null with a <div> containing an <h2> for a title, an <input> for username entry, and a <button> for login.
steps.expectedOutcome: The login form appears when the user is not logged in, with a heading, input field, and button.
successCriteria: The false branch of the ternary contains a <div> with an <h2>, an <input>, and a <button>.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track. Make sure the false branch contains a <div> with all three elements: heading, input, and button.
steps.feedbackWrong: Check the false branch of your ternary. It should return a <div> containing an <h2>, an <input>, and a <button> instead of null.

steps.title: Wire login button to handler
steps.instruction: Add an onClick handler to the login button that calls the handleLogin function.
steps.hint: Use the onClick attribute on the button element and set it to call handleLogin.
steps.analogousExample:
// Example: wiring a button to a handler
<button onClick={handleSubmit}>Submit</button>
steps.expectedOutcome: The login button should now trigger the handleLogin function when clicked.
successCriteria: The login button has an onClick attribute set to handleLogin.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close. Make sure the onClick attribute is set to call handleLogin.
steps.feedbackWrong: The login button is not properly wired to the handler. Check the onClick attribute.

steps.title: Create dashboard markup with logout button
steps.instruction: In the true branch of the ternary (where the welcome message currently appears), add a logout button that calls the handleLogout function when clicked.
steps.hint: Add a button element inside the true branch, right after the welcome paragraph. Use the onClick prop to call handleLogout.
steps.analogousExample:
// Example: adding a logout button

Welcome, user!
steps.expectedOutcome: When isLoggedIn is true, the UI will show both the welcome message and a logout button that triggers the logout handler.
successCriteria: A logout button with onClick={handleLogout} is present in the true branch of the ternary.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You've added a button, but make sure it's in the correct branch (when isLoggedIn is true) and calls handleLogout when clicked.
steps.feedbackWrong: The logout button is missing or not properly connected to the logout handler. Check that you've added the button with onClick={handleLogout} inside the true branch of the ternary.
